slides.0.title: Distillation and Maturation in Depth
slides.0.subtitle: Lees, cuts, and the chemistry inside the cask
slides.1.title: Variables in distillation
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Distilling on the lees
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Lees are dead yeast cells left after fermentation. Distilling on the lees is generally linked to a nuttier, creamier and more complex spirit, while filtering gives a cleaner one. Lees contain fatty acid esters relevant to later rancio, but solids can stick and burn on the still, causing off-flavours (alcademics)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Time and strength
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Base wine is around 9%, rising to about 30% after the first run and about 70–72% after the second; each run takes about 12 hours, so work is continuous through the season (alcademics; as in Level 1, exact figures vary slightly by source)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Cuts at both stages
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Heads and tails cuts are made after both distillations; where to cut is a stylistic decision for the distiller (alcademics)
slides.1.content: Reports on which houses use lees conflict, so this is not tested.
slides.2.title: Four processes in oak
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Extraction and subtraction
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Extraction: wood compounds dissolve into the spirit, adding colour, flavour and structure. Subtraction: the charred layer acts like activated carbon and removes harsh sulphur compounds (WSET Level 2, Spirits & Distilling)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Oxidation and evaporation
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Oxidation: slow oxygen ingress softens the spirit and builds esters. Evaporation: water and alcohol escape through the staves, the angels' share (WSET Level 2)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Compounds and flavours
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Lignin yields vanillin (vanilla), eugenol (clove) and guaiacol (smoky); toasted hemicellulose gives caramelised sugars and furfural; oak lactones add coconut and woody notes; tannins dissolve fastest in the first 6–12 months in new oak (Spirits & Distilling)
slides.2.content: Maturation is not linear: quality often rises, dips, then reaches a new plateau.
slides.3.title: Oak type and climate
slides.3.highlights.0.title: American vs European oak
slides.3.highlights.0.content: American white oak is high in lactones and vanillin and lower in tannin; European oak (robur/petraea) has more ellagitannins, giving structure and dried fruit, clove and spice (WSET Level 2). Cognac uses French oak; Jerez uses American oak
slides.3.highlights.1.title: New versus used casks
slides.3.highlights.1.content: New oak extracts fastest and most intensely; refill casks have little extractive power, letting the base spirit show (WSET Level 2). This explains Cognac's move from new to older casks
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Warehouse climate
slides.3.highlights.2.content: In dry air water evaporates faster so ABV rises; in humid air ABV falls; tropical maturation is much faster (WSET Level 2)
slides.3.content: Diploma often asks why the same age tastes different in different regions.
